title: US Freezes Immigrant Visa Interviews Worldwide Days After Court Struck Down 75-Country Ban
excerpt: State Department cites global consular training on public charge screening as it pauses appointments with no timeline for resumption.
body:
• The State Department has paused immigrant visa appointments at all US embassies and consulates worldwide, citing a global training initiative on public charge screening
  • The freeze comes just days after a federal judge struck down the administration's earlier policy suspending immigrant visas from 75 countries as exceeding Secretary of State Marco Rubio's authority
  • No timeline has been given for resumption; applicants with scheduled interviews have received emails that appointments are being rescheduled
  • Separately, the administration recently proposed a permanent $103,265 H-1B visa fee that would reshape skilled worker immigration costs

The Trump administration has frozen immigrant visa interviews at US embassies and consulates around the world, the latest disruption in an escalating immigration crackdown that has left thousands of applicants in limbo with no clear timeline for when processing will resume.

A State Department spokesperson said Tuesday that the department launched a "global training initiative" at all diplomatic posts, with visa appointments being "adjusted to accommodate the training." The initiative focuses on ensuring consular officers can screen out applicants deemed likely to become dependent on US public benefits.

Timing Raises Questions

The worldwide pause lands less than a week after US District Judge Jeannette Vargas in Manhattan struck down the administration's earlier policy that had suspended immigrant visa issuance from 75 countries since January. Vargas ruled the policy was "contrary to law" and exceeded Rubio's statutory authority.

https://x.com/TheCradleMedia/status/2092538157107417322

The judge found that consular officers had been ordered to refuse applications even when an applicant "provides additional evidence that demonstrates he or she overcomes the public charge refusal." A separate ruling by Judge Amit Mehta in Washington earlier found the same policy unlawful, though that decision provided relief only to one individual plaintiff.

Bloomberg Tax reported that the new pause is directly connected to a State Department training initiative launched in early August focused on updated "public charge" guidance — the same legal basis underpinning the struck-down 75-country ban.

Open-Ended Delay

The Financial Times first reported that immigrant visa applicants with scheduled interviews at US embassies have received emails informing them their appointments are being rescheduled, with a promise of future notice for a new date. No end date for the training period has been announced.

"Many affected applicants had already spent thousands of dollars and disrupted their lives to attend scheduled interviews, only to have their appointments cancelled at the last minute."

— Brian Simmons, immigration attorney at Fragomen

Immigration attorneys and human rights advocates argue the open-ended delays impose real financial and emotional strain on separated families. The pause affects both family-based and employment-based immigrant visa applicants who are required to complete processing outside the United States.

A Broader Crackdown

The visa freeze is the latest in a series of moves disrupting legal immigration pathways under the current administration. Since returning to office, Trump has pursued visa and green card revocations linked in some cases to political activity, expanded social media vetting for student visa applicants, and halted scheduling of new student visa appointments earlier this year.

This week also saw The Videshi report on the administration's proposed permanent $103,265 H-1B fee, which NASSCOM has strongly opposed, arguing it would devastate Indian IT firms and skilled workers who form the backbone of H-1B applications.

What It Means for Indian Applicants

Indian nationals represent one of the largest pools of immigrant visa applicants globally, spanning family-sponsored, employment-based, and diversity visa categories. The pause compounds existing backlogs — Indian applicants in some employment-based categories already face wait times stretching decades due to per-country caps.

For families separated by the immigration process, each week of delay carries concrete consequences: missed school enrollments, deferred medical care, and the grinding uncertainty of indefinite separation. The State Department's refusal to provide a timeline only deepens that burden.
